title: Working backwards from a derivative
objectives: Find antiderivatives of the standard functions.
Explain the $+C$ and fix it from a starting value.

screens.prose: We want a function $F$ whose slope at every $x$ is $2x$. Try $F(x) = ax^2$. Drag P along the curve to read slopes, and set $a$ with the slider.
screens.question: Which $a$ makes the slope of $F$ equal $2x$ at every $x$?

hints.text: Put P at $x = 1$. The target slope there is 2.
The slope of $ax^2$ is $2ax$.
$2ax = 2x$ at every $x$ needs $a = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the slope with the target $2x$ at two or three points.

byKey.two: With $a = 2$ the slope is $4x$, double the target. You matched the 2 in $2x$, but differentiating brings down another 2.
byKey.half: With $a = 0.5$ the slope is $x$, half the target.

explain.text: With $a = 1$ the slope at every P matches $2x$. We ran differentiation backwards: from the slope $2x$ we recovered $x^2$. Such an $F$ is called an **antiderivative** of $2x$.

screens.prose: Now the target slope is $x^3$. Try $F(x) = ax^4$.
screens.question: Which $a$ makes the slope of $F$ equal $x^3$ at every $x$?

hints.text: The slope of $ax^4$ is $4ax^3$.
At $x = 1$ the target slope is 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate $ax^4$ and match it to $x^3$.

byKey.third: You divided by 3, the old power. Differentiating $x^4$ brings down a 4, so divide by 4.
byKey.one: With $a = 1$ the slope is $4x^3$, four times too big.

explain.text: Differentiating $x^4$ brings down a 4, so we divide by 4 to cancel it: $F(x) = \tfrac{x^4}{4}$. The pattern: raise the power by one, then divide by the new power.

screens.prose: $x^2$ has slope $2x$. So does $x^2 + C$ for any constant $C$. Slide $C$ and watch the slope at P.
screens.question: As you slide $C$, what happens to the slope at P?

options.text: It stays the same: the curve only moves up or down

options.why: You watched P rise. The slope label reads the same at every $C$, because the whole curve shifts up rigidly.

options.text: It turns negative when $C$ is negative
options.why: A negative $C$ lowers the curve but keeps its shape, so the slope at P keeps its sign.

hints.text: Fix P at $x = 1$ and move only $C$.
Read the slope label at $C = -3$ and at $C = 3$.
The slope reads 2.00 at every $C$: shifting the curve does not tilt it.

feedback.correct: A constant shifts the curve without tilting it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep P still and read the slope at several values of $C$.

explain.text: Shifting a curve up or down leaves every slope unchanged, since a constant has derivative 0. So $2x$ has a whole family of antiderivatives, $x^2 + C$. We write $\int 2x\,dx = x^2 + C$, the **indefinite integral**.

screens.prose: Raise the power by one, then divide by the new power. Check your answer by differentiating it.
screens.question: Find $\int x^4\,dx$. Leave out the $+C$.

hints.text: What power must $F$ have, if differentiating lowers it to 4?
Try $x^5$: its derivative is $5x^4$.
$5x^4$ is five times too big, so take $\tfrac{x^5}{5}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Raise the power to 5, divide by 5, then differentiate to check.

byKey.old-power: You divided by 4, the old power. Differentiate $\tfrac{x^5}{4}$: you get $\tfrac{5}{4}x^4$, too big. Divide by the new power, 5.
byKey.no-divide: The derivative of $x^5$ is $5x^4$, five times too big. Divide by 5.
byKey.derivative: You differentiated $x^4$. We want the function whose derivative is $x^4$.

explain.text: Differentiating $\tfrac{x^5}{5}$ gives $\tfrac{5x^4}{5} = x^4$. So $\int x^4\,dx = \tfrac{x^5}{5} + C$. The new curve rises where $x^4 > 0$, which is everywhere except 0.

screens.prose: At $n = -1$ the power rule gives $\dfrac{x^0}{0}$, which is meaningless. We need another function with slope $\dfrac{1}{x}$. Drag P along $\ln x$ and compare its slope with $\tfrac{1}{x}$.
screens.question: Which function is an antiderivative of $\dfrac{1}{x}$ for $x > 0$?

options.why: You applied the power rule at $n = -1$. That divides by zero, so it names no function.
That is the derivative of $\tfrac{1}{x}$. We want the function whose derivative is $\tfrac{1}{x}$.
You lowered the power instead of raising it. Its derivative is $x^{-3}$, not $x^{-1}$.

hints.text: Drag P and compare the slope label with $\tfrac{1}{x}$ in the caption.
At $x = 2$ the slope of $\ln x$ is 0.5.
The derivative of $\ln x$ is $\tfrac{1}{x}$, so $\ln x$ is an antiderivative.

feedback.correct: $(\ln x)' = \tfrac{1}{x}$, so $\ln x$ fills the gap at $n = -1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the slope of $\ln x$ at a few points and compare it with $\tfrac{1}{x}$.

explain.text: $\ln x$ has slope $\tfrac{1}{x}$ at every $x > 0$. For $x < 0$, $\ln(-x)$ has slope $\tfrac{-1}{-x} = \tfrac{1}{x}$ too. Together: $\int \tfrac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln|x| + C$.

screens.prose: The graph shows $\sin x$ and $\cos x$. Drag P along $\cos x$ and compare its slope with $\sin x$.
screens.question: What is $\int \sin x\,dx$?

options.why: The slope of $\cos x$ is $-\sin x$: the label and the caption have opposite signs. So $\cos x$ gives the wrong sign.
You treated $\sin x$ like a power of $x$. The power rule works on $x^n$ only.
Its slope is $-\cos x$, not $\sin x$. Differentiate your answer to check.

hints.text: Compare the slope label with the caption at a few points.
The slope of $\cos x$ is always $-\sin x$.
So the slope of $-\cos x$ is $\sin x$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate each option and see which gives $\sin x$.

explain.text: At every P the slope of $\cos x$ was minus the value of $\sin x$. Flipping the sign, $(-\cos x)' = \sin x$. In the same way $(\sin x)' = \cos x$ gives $\int \cos x\,dx = \sin x + C$.

screens.prose: Since $(e^x)' = e^x$, it is tempting to write $\int e^{2x}\,dx = e^{2x} + C$. The graph shows $e^{2x}$. Drag P and compare its slope with its height.
screens.question: Find $\int e^{2x}\,dx$. Leave out the $+C$.

hints.text: Differentiate $e^{2x}$. What extra factor does the chain rule bring out?
The slope of $e^{2x}$ is twice its height.
$(e^{2x})' = 2e^{2x}$, so $\tfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}$ has derivative $e^{2x}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate your answer: you should get exactly $e^{2x}$.

byKey.copy: You copied the rule for $e^x$. The chain rule gives $(e^{2x})' = 2e^{2x}$, twice too big.
byKey.times-two: $2e^{2x}$ is the derivative of $e^{2x}$. We want the function whose derivative is $e^{2x}$, so divide by 2.
byKey.power-rule: You treated $e^{2x}$ as a power of $x$. Here the variable is in the exponent, so the power rule does not apply.

explain.text: The caption showed the slope is always twice the height: $(e^{2x})' = 2e^{2x}$. Halving fixes it: $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}\right)' = e^{2x}$. Always check an antiderivative by differentiating it.

screens.prose: Now generalise the fix to $\int e^{kx}\,dx$, for any constant $k \neq 0$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Guess $F(x) = e^{kx}$: then $F'(x) = k\,e^{kx}$, by the chain rule
That is $k$ times too big, so try $F(x) = \dfrac{1}{k}e^{kx}$, which needs $k \neq 0$
$F'(x) = \dfrac{1}{k} \cdot k\,e^{kx} = e^{kx}$, since a constant factor rides through the derivative
So $\int e^{kx}\,dx = \dfrac{e^{kx}}{k} + C$, adding the constant for the whole family

hints.text: Start from the natural first guess.
The guess is off by a factor. Fix it, then check the fix.
Guess $e^{kx}$, divide by $k$, differentiate to check, then add $C$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The fix comes from what the first guess gets wrong.

byKey.fix: You can only see the factor $k$ to divide out after differentiating the first guess.
byKey.check: The check differentiates the fixed guess, so the fix must come first.
byKey.family: The conclusion comes last, once the check has passed.

explain.text: Differentiating $e^{kx}$ brings out $k$, so we divide by $k$ and check. With $k = 2$ this gives $\tfrac{1}{2}e^{2x}$, as on the last screen. At $k = 0$ the rule breaks: $e^{0x} = 1$, and $\int 1\,dx = x + C$.

screens.prose: Every antiderivative so far came from reading a derivative backwards: $$\int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \quad (n \neq -1), \qquad \int \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln|x| + C$$ $$\int e^{kx}\,dx = \frac{e^{kx}}{k} + C, \quad \int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x + C, \quad \int \cos x\,dx = \sin x + C$$
screens.question: Match each function to an antiderivative.

feedback.correct: Each antiderivative differentiates back to its function.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate each token you placed and compare.

byKey.d-cos: $\cos x$ differentiates to $-\sin x$, so it fits no slot. $\sin x$ needs $-\cos x$.
byKey.d-3exp: $3e^{3x}$ is the derivative of $e^{3x}$, not an antiderivative. Divide by 3 instead.
byKey.d-sq: $-\tfrac{1}{x^2}$ is the derivative of $\tfrac{1}{x}$. Its antiderivative is $\ln|x|$.

explain.text: Each pair is a derivative fact read backwards: $(\sin x)' = \cos x$, $(-\cos x)' = \sin x$, $(\ln|x|)' = \tfrac{1}{x}$ and $\left(\tfrac{1}{3}e^{3x}\right)' = e^{3x}$. The leftover tokens are derivatives, not antiderivatives.

screens.prose: A desk carries £2k of P&L into the session. Its P&L rate is $r(t) = 3 - \tfrac{t}{2}$, in £k per hour, $t$ hours in. Cumulative P&L $P(t)$ has $P'(t) = r(t)$ and $P(0) = 2$.

state.caption: Antiderivatives $3t - \tfrac{t^2}{4} + C$ for two values of $C$

screens.question: What is $P(4)$, in £k?

hints.text: Find an antiderivative of $3 - \tfrac{t}{2}$, then fix $C$ with $P(0) = 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate the rate, then use $P(0) = 2$ to fix the constant.

byKey.no-c: You left out the constant. $P(0) = 2$ fixes $C = 2$, the P&L carried in.
byKey.rate: 1 is the rate $r(4)$, in £k per hour. We want the P&L itself.
byKey.no-divide: You integrated $\tfrac{t}{2}$ as $\tfrac{t^2}{2}$. Raising the power gives $t^2$, divided by 2 twice: $\tfrac{t^2}{4}$.

explain.text: The antiderivatives $3t - \tfrac{t^2}{4} + C$ form a family of curves. The carried-in £2k picks the one through $(0, 2)$, so $C = 2$. Then $P(4) = 12 - 4 + 2 = 10$, so £10k.

ideas: An antiderivative of $f$ is any $F$ with $F' = f$: a derivative fact read backwards.
Antiderivatives come as a family $F + C$, because shifting a curve up or down keeps every slope. A starting value fixes $C$.
Check every antiderivative by differentiating it. The chain rule is why $\int e^{kx}\,dx = \tfrac{e^{kx}}{k} + C$.
summary.trap: Divide by the new power $n + 1$, not the old one. And $\int e^{2x}\,dx$ is $\tfrac{1}{2}e^{2x} + C$, not $e^{2x} + C$.

options.why: You lowered the power. Antiderivatives raise it: $-3 + 1 = -2$.
You divided by the old power, $-3$. Divide by the new power, $-2$.
The log rule is for $x^{-1}$ only. Here $n = -3$, so the power rule works.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Raise the power by one and divide by the new power.

explain.text: Raising $-3$ by one gives $-2$, so $\int x^{-3}\,dx = \tfrac{x^{-2}}{-2} + C = -\tfrac{1}{2x^2} + C$. Check: the derivative of $-\tfrac{1}{2}x^{-2}$ is $x^{-3}$.

options.why: You divided by 0.04, but $k = -0.04$. The minus sign stays.
You differentiated. Undoing the chain rule divides by $k$; it does not multiply.
You copied the rule for $e^x$. The chain rule brings out $-0.04$, which you must divide out.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\int e^{kt}\,dt = \tfrac{e^{kt}}{k} + C$ with $k = -0.04$.

explain.text: With $k = -0.04$, $\tfrac{1}{k} = -25$, so the antiderivative is $-25e^{-0.04t} + C$. Check: its derivative is $-25 \times (-0.04)e^{-0.04t} = e^{-0.04t}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate, then use $F(1) = 5$ to find $C$.

byKey.slope: 24 is $F'(2)$, the slope. We want the value $F(2)$.

quiz.prose: On $x > 0$, $\ln x$ is an antiderivative of $\dfrac{1}{x}$.
quiz.question: What about on $x < 0$?

options.text: $\ln x$ is undefined there, but $\ln(-x)$ works

options.why: You extended $\ln x$ to negative $x$, where it is not defined.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate $\ln(-x)$ with the chain rule.

explain.text: $\ln x$ needs $x > 0$. For $x < 0$, the chain rule gives $(\ln(-x))' = \tfrac{-1}{-x} = \tfrac{1}{x}$. Both cases are $\ln|x|$.
